title: Django and DRF in one lesson
bridge: A Django model, a DRF serializer and a viewset are like a Prisma model, a zod schema and an API route handler. Except: Django generates the migrations and the admin from the model. A viewset gives you all the CRUD routes at once through a router, so you never write the route table by hand.
intro: fcp's cloud is a Django project with Django REST Framework (DRF) on top. Every API test in G7 posts JSON into a viewset, which runs a serializer, which saves a model. This lesson follows one request through those three layers and shows how pytest-django gives each test a clean database.

picture.caption: One POST travels through the router, the viewset and the serializer into a model row, and comes back as JSON.

steps.text: the router maps POST /api/notes/ to the viewset's create action
the viewset hands the body to the serializer, which validates it
the ORM writes one row inside the test's transaction
the response is 201 with the saved note as JSON

p: A Django project is a folder with manage.py (the CLI), a settings module and one or more apps. An app is a package with models.py, views.py and migrations/. settings.py lists the apps in INSTALLED_APPS. An app that is not listed does not exist for Django, and its models fail with an app_label error.

In fcp the project is cloud/rhinoCloud/, and the settings module is rhinoCloud.rhinoDjango.settings. The main app is rhinoCore/. It has models/, views/, serializers/, services/, celery_tasks/, migrations/ and tests/ as folders instead of single files. The names are the same as in the tiny project below, only bigger.
sections.because: When a ticket says rhinoCore/serializers or rhinoDjango/urls.py, you should see the Django shape behind the path.

p: A model is a class whose fields describe a table. Django's ORM (object-relational mapper) turns Note.objects.create(title="x") into an INSERT and Note.objects.filter(title="x") into a SELECT. You never write SQL.

A migration is a Python file that describes one change to the schema. makemigrations compares your models with the last migration and writes the next file; migrate applies it to the database. Migrations are committed and numbered: rhinoCore has 228 of them. fcp's cloud CI runs makemigrations --check --dry-run to fail when someone changed a model and forgot the migration.
sections.because: Agents will change models, and G7-15 lints the migrations they produce. So you need to know what a migration is and where it comes from.

code.text:
from django.db import models


class Note(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    body = models.TextField(blank=True)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

notes.text: Subclassing models.Model makes this a table called notes_note (app name, underscore, class name).
A field is a class attribute with a field type. Django adds an id primary key by itself.
blank=True means the API may send an empty string. It is validation, not a database rule.
auto_now_add fills the value on insert, so the serializer marks it read-only.

sections.see:
$ uv run python manage.py makemigrations notes
Migrations for 'notes':
  notes/migrations/0001_initial.py
    + Create model Note
$ uv run python manage.py sqlmigrate notes 0001
CREATE TABLE "notes_note" ("id" integer NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, "title" varchar(120) NOT NULL, ...);
sections.ifInstead: If instead you see RuntimeError: Model class notes.models.Note doesn't declare an explicit app_label, the app is missing from INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py.

p: A serializer is the zod schema of DRF. It turns JSON into validated Python values on the way in, and a model instance into JSON on the way out. A ModelSerializer reads the field list from the model, so you list which fields to expose and which are read-only.

When the body is invalid, serializer.is_valid() is false and the viewset returns 400 with a dict of field errors. This is why G7-06 wants test data created through the API: a factory writes rows and skips all of this.
sections.because: Most API bugs live in serializers (a renamed field, a new required one), and G7-11's OpenAPI check reads its schema from them.

code.text:
from rest_framework import serializers

from .models import Note


class NoteSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Note
        fields = ["id", "title", "body", "created_at"]
        read_only_fields = ["id", "created_at"]

notes.text: A relative import: the models module next to this file.
Meta is an inner class Django and DRF use for configuration; it is not a type annotation.
The fields the API shows and accepts. Removing one here is a breaking API change.
Shown in responses, rejected in requests. A field that becomes required would also be a breaking change.

p: A viewset is a class with one method per action: list, retrieve, create, update, partial_update, destroy. ModelViewSet gives you all six from a queryset and a serializer class. A router takes the viewset and registers the URL patterns: GET and POST on /api/notes/, GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE on /api/notes/<id>/.
fcp's URLs are versioned under /api/v2/ (and a connect API). The router lives in rhinoDjango/urls.py together with the OpenAPI schema view at /docs/v2/openapi/ that G7-11 exports.
sections.because: When a test calls GET /api/v2/projects/, you need to know which class answers and how the path was built.

code.text:
from rest_framework import viewsets

from .models import Note
from .serializers import NoteSerializer


class NoteViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Note.objects.order_by("-created_at")
    serializer_class = NoteSerializer


# mysite/urls.py
from django.urls import include, path
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter

from notes.views import NoteViewSet

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register("notes", NoteViewSet)

urlpatterns = [path("api/", include(router.urls))]

notes.text: Six CRUD actions for free. Override one method (for example create) when you need custom behaviour.
The queryset is the base query every action starts from; permissions usually filter it further.
A DefaultRouter also serves an index page at /api/ that lists the endpoints.
The prefix notes becomes /notes/ and /notes/<pk>/.
Mounted under api/, so the final paths are /api/notes/ and /api/notes/<id>/.

p: DRF's APIClient is a fake browser: client.post(path, data, format="json") runs the whole stack in-process and returns a response with status_code and .json(). No server, no network. pytest-django wires Django into pytest.
It reads DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE from pytest.ini and creates a test database. It wraps every test marked django_db in a transaction that is rolled back at the end. Each test starts clean.

Authentication: client.force_authenticate(user) skips login for a unit test. G7-06 does the opposite on purpose: its in-process client fetches a real JWT from auth/obtain_token, so the auth path is tested too.
sections.because: This is the shape of every test in tests_api: a client, a call, an assert on what the caller sees.

notes.text: pytestmark applies a marker to every test in the file. Without django_db, any database access raises an error.
format="json" sends a JSON body. The call runs the router, viewset, serializer and model in this process.
Assert on what the caller sees: status code, then fields. Not on which internal function ran.
The note from the previous test is gone: its transaction was rolled back.

sections.ifInstead: If instead you see Database access not allowed, use the "django_db" mark. Add pytestmark = pytest.mark.django_db to the file, or the marker to the test.

sections.h: The test database and the template trick
p: pytest-django creates a database named test_<name>, runs every migration into it, runs the tests, and drops it. --reuse-db keeps it between runs. With xdist each worker gets its own copy, test_<name>_gw0, test_<name>_gw1, so workers never see each other's rows.
Running 228 migrations per worker is slow. G7-02 overrides the django_db_setup fixture. One worker migrates into a template database once.

Then every worker gets CREATE DATABASE test_api_gw1 TEMPLATE api_tpl_<hash>, a Postgres copy that takes seconds. The template name is a hash of the migration file names, so a new migration builds a new template. This is a Postgres feature; SQLite in the lab has no templates, which is why the lab uses --reuse-db instead.
sections.because: The 3-minute target for the whole API layer depends on this fixture. You will read it when something about the database setup breaks.

code.text:
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def django_db_setup(django_db_blocker, worker_id):
    db = settings.DATABASES["default"]
    worker_db = f"test_api_{worker_id}"  # worker_id is "master" when xdist is off
    with django_db_blocker.unblock(), connection._nodb_cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_lock(7007)")  # one worker builds the template
        cur.execute("SELECT 1 FROM pg_database WHERE datname = %s", [TEMPLATE_DB])
        if cur.fetchone() is None:
            cur.execute(f'CREATE DATABASE "{TEMPLATE_DB}"')
            db["NAME"] = TEMPLATE_DB
            call_command("migrate", verbosity=0)
            call_command("loaddata", str(CORE / "fixtures" / "initial_data_prod_aws.json"), verbosity=0)
            connections.close_all()
        cur.execute(f'DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "{worker_db}"')
        cur.execute(f'CREATE DATABASE "{worker_db}" TEMPLATE "{TEMPLATE_DB}"')
    db["NAME"] = worker_db
    yield

notes.text: Same name as pytest-django's own fixture, so this one replaces it. Session scope: once per worker process.
worker_id comes from xdist (p10-2). django_db_blocker is pytest-django's guard against database access outside tests.
A cursor on the postgres maintenance database, because you cannot create a database from inside itself.
An advisory lock: a named lock in Postgres. Four workers start at once; only one builds the template, the others wait.
The 228 migrations run here, once, into the template.
The Postgres copy: a new database with the template's tables and rows, in seconds.
From here on, this worker's Django connection points at its own copy.

callout.text: The full G7-02 sketch also runs createcachetable (fcp's settings use a database cache table). The lines here are the ones that explain the mechanism.

p: fcp's cloud also runs Celery (a background job queue) and talks to on-prem clients over gRPC. Both are faked in p10-4. The existing 1,900 unit tests use Django's runner and factory_boy; they keep running as they are. The new API layer uses what you saw here: APIClient, pytest-django and the template database.

lab.faded: Add a field done = models.BooleanField(default=False) to Note and to the serializer's fields. Write a test that creates a note, sends PATCH /api/notes/<id>/ with {"done": true} and asserts the response shows done as true. Run the tests: they fail until you create the migration. Creating it is the step left for you; makemigrations --check tells you when you are done.
lab.alone: Add a second model Tag(name) with its own serializer and viewset registered as "tags". Write two tests. POST creates a tag and returns 201. GET /api/tags/ returns one row after that POST, and zero rows in a fresh test. Run them with -n 2 and with --reuse-db.
lab.done: pytest -n 2 passes with both models, makemigrations --check --dry-run prints No changes detected, and a fresh test sees an empty list.

quiz.q: You add a field to a model, run the tests, and they fail with no such column. What did you forget?

options.why: A fresh database would still lack the column, because no migration adds it.

options.text: Running makemigrations to write the migration that adds the column.
options.why: Models describe the schema, migrations change it. fcp's CI runs makemigrations --check to catch exactly this.

options.text: Adding the field to the serializer.
options.why: That controls the API shape; the database error comes from the missing migration.

quiz.q: Why does G7-06 create test data through the API instead of writing rows with a factory?

options.text: Factories are slower than HTTP calls.
options.why: Factories are faster; speed is not the reason.

options.text: Rows written through the API pass the serializer validation and the permission checks that a factory skips.
options.why: A factory can create a state the API would never allow, and tests on that state prove little.
rhinoCore/tests use factory_boy and keep doing so.

quiz.q: With pytest -n 4 and the G7-02 conftest, how many times do the 228 migrations run?

options.why: That is the slow default this fixture replaces.

options.text: Once, into the template database; each worker then copies the template with CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE.
options.why: The advisory lock makes one worker build it; the others wait and copy.

options.text: Zero times; the tests use SQLite.
options.why: The API layer runs on Postgres, like CI and production.

words.plain: A Python class whose fields describe a database table; the ORM turns calls on it into SQL.
A numbered Python file that describes one schema change; makemigrations writes it, migrate applies it.
The DRF class that validates incoming JSON and renders model instances as JSON; the zod schema of the API.
A class with one method per CRUD action; ModelViewSet gives all six from a queryset and a serializer.
The DRF object that turns a viewset into URL patterns like /api/notes/ and /api/notes/<id>/.
DRF's in-process test client: it runs a request through the whole stack with no server.
A Postgres database that other databases are copied from with CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE; migrated once, copied per worker.

tickets.why: The tests_api layer is pytest-django, APIClient and the template-database conftest explained here.
The CI job runs that layer with a throw-away Postgres service. So you need to know what the tests need from the database.
The in-process RhinoAPI swaps requests for APIClient.generic and fetches a real JWT; this lesson shows what APIClient does.
The SDK smoke test uses pytest-django's live_server, a real HTTP server over the same test database.

remember: Model is the table, serializer is the schema, and viewset plus router is the route. APIClient runs it all in-process, and pytest-django rolls each test back.
